# Climate Microinsurance: Distribution & Business-Model Architecture
## Multi-Region Pilot Design — East Africa, South Asia, Central America (2026–2030)

*Parameter note: premium rates, subsidy regimes, mobile-money penetration, reinsurance pricing and index data availability move fast and differ by district, not by country. Figures below are calibrated to a mid-size composite insurer running a $2.5M first-year pilot and are illustrative of magnitude and method. The decision architecture — matching rules, gates, kill criteria — is the deliverable; every number is a placeholder for a client-specific input.*

---

## 1. Executive Summary

**Four findings drive the recommendation, and three of them contradict the standard playbook.**

**1. This is not a distribution problem. It is a unit-economics problem disguised as one.** At a $12–16 annual premium, no channel that has to *sell* the product can ever be affordable. Acquisition cost must land under ~$1.50/policy/year fully loaded, which is 3–8x below what any dedicated agent, broker or app-install funnel achieves. The only viable channels are those where the customer is **already transacting for another reason** — input credit, harvest aggregation, mobile-money float, remittance receipt, loan disbursement. The correct question is not "who can sell this?" but **"who is already paying the acquisition cost for something else, and what will they accept as their share?"** Distribution partners are cost carriers, not salesforces.

**2. Trust is not one thing, and each region is short of a different component.** Decompose it into three: *trust that the product pays* (product credibility), *trust that the intermediary won't steal or mis-sell* (fiduciary credibility), and *trust in the measurement that triggers payment* (index credibility). East Africa is short of product credibility (a decade of disappointing index products); South Asia is short of index credibility and drowning in state-scheme distortion; Central America is short of fiduciary credibility outside a narrow set of cooperatives. **Matching the intermediary to the scarce component — not to reach or cost — is the core distribution rule.**

**3. Payout *frequency* builds the book; payout *adequacy* protects the balance sheet. Design for both explicitly, and stop optimizing the index for total error.** Microinsurance renewal behavior responds to observed payout probability, not expected value. Standard actuarial calibration minimizes combined false-positive and false-negative rates; that is the wrong objective here, because the two errors are **wildly asymmetric in commercial cost**. A payout when there was no loss costs money once. A loss with no payout destroys the franchise in that village permanently and contaminates neighboring wards. Set strikes loose, accept a higher false-positive rate, and fund the difference as marketing spend rather than pretending it's a pricing error.

**4. Start meso, not retail — but with contractual pass-through, or you build nothing.** Insuring the *aggregator's* portfolio (cooperative, MFI, input-credit provider) collapses acquisition cost by ~80% and eliminates individual claims adjudication entirely. Its defect is that the farmer never sees a payout and no consumer-facing trust asset accumulates. The fix is a **visible pass-through obligation** — loan forgiveness or next-season input credit, farmer-notified by SMS, published at group level — which converts a B2B contract into a retail trust-building instrument at B2B cost.

### Recommended architecture

| Region | Anchor channel | Business model (2026–28) | Migration path (2029–30) | Faith/community role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **East Africa** | Mobile-money wallet rider (MNO) + dairy/coffee coops | Embedded retail micro-premium; meso for coop input credit | Retail-dominant; MNO as billing rail | Endorsement + grievance panels only |
| **South Asia** | MFI / SHG federation portfolio cover | **Meso-first**, plus basis-risk *top-up* wrapper on state schemes | Selective retail via fintech for non-crop perils (heat, livestock) | Minimal; SHG federations carry legitimacy |
| **Central America** | Coffee/cocoa cooperative + **diaspora remittance-funded premium** | Meso on coop portfolio; retail premium paid by US-based family member | Remittance-rider retail at scale | High — parish networks for legitimacy & disputes, never for cash |

**Do not fund in the base case:** standalone fintech app acquisition in any region; dedicated agent networks; any product in a district that fails the data-maturity gate (§6).

---

## 2. Framing: Four Decisions Usually Collapsed Into One

| Question | Wrong framing | Right framing |
|---|---|---|
| **What are we selling?** | "Climate insurance for smallholders" | Which *peril–crop–district* triples have data good enough to price and a loss event the farmer already recognizes as insurable? |
| **Who distributes?** | "Which channel has the most reach?" | Which institution already carries the transaction cost, and which trust deficit does it repair? |
| **Who is the customer?** | The farmer | In year 1: the aggregator, the lender, the subsidy agency, or the migrant remitter. The farmer becomes the customer in year 3. |
| **What are we optimizing?** | Policies sold | **Persistency.** A one-year policyholder destroys ~$2 of value; a three-year policyholder creates ~$4. Acquisition is a cost center; renewal is the entire business. |

---

## 3. The Binding Constraint: Unit Economics

### 3.1 Retail embedded policy — illustrative P&L per policy-year

| Line | Amount | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Gross written premium | **$14.00** | Sum insured ~$150 (≈1 ha input cost), rate ~9% |
| Expected claims | ($8.40) | Target loss ratio 60% |
| Reinsurance risk margin (net of recoveries) | ($1.30) | Covariate peril; cat XoL + quota share |
| Channel commission | ($2.10) | 15% — the MNO/coop share |
| Policy admin, KYC, payments | ($0.90) | Achievable only at >250k policies on shared platform |
| Acquisition & farmer education (yr 1) | ($1.40) | Amortized field training, radio, demo payouts |
| Cost of capital | ($0.55) | High-capital line: correlated risk |
| **Year-1 result** | **($0.65)** | Loss-making |
| **Year-2+ result (renewed)** | **+$1.15** | Acquisition falls to ~$0.20; admin scales |

**Implication:** breakeven requires ~2.1 policy-years. Observed microinsurance renewal after a *non-payout* year is commonly 20–40%. **At 40% persistency this book never earns its capital. At 70% it clears cost of capital by year 4.** Everything in the design below is downstream of that single number.

### 3.2 Meso policy — the same 5,000 farmers, one contract

| Line | Retail (5,000 policies) | Meso (1 contract) |
|---|---|---|
| GWP | $70,000 | $62,000 |
| Acquisition | $7,000 | $1,200 (amortized B2B sale) |
| Admin + claims handling | $4,500 | $600 |
| Commission | $10,500 | $3,100 (5%) |
| **Expense ratio** | **~32%** | **~8%** |
| Farmer-visible payout | Yes | **No — unless engineered** |

Meso buys you a viable expense ratio and a three-year runway to build data. It does not buy you a market. The pass-through obligation (§7.3) is what makes it strategic rather than merely profitable.

---

## 4. The Trust Decomposition and the Matching Rule

| Trust component | What fails when it's absent | Institutions that supply it |
|---|---|---|
| **Product credibility** — "will this thing ever pay?" | No first purchase; word-of-mouth poison from prior failed index schemes | Prior payout record; public payout registry; government or donor guarantee; visible peer payouts |
| **Fiduciary credibility** — "will my money reach the insurer?" | Premium leakage, agent fraud, non-renewal after a single bad agent | Cooperatives with audited books; MNO wallets (auditable rails); MFIs with repayment relationships |
| **Index credibility** — "is the satellite/rain gauge telling the truth about *my* field?" | Basis-risk disputes; mass lapse after a false negative | Community validation panels; third-party calculation agent; picture-based ground truth; area-yield cross-checks |

**Matching rule:** *Assign the primary channel to the region's scarcest trust component; assign secondary institutions to the others; never let one institution supply all three.* Concentrating trust functions creates a single point of franchise failure and makes the intermediary un-fireable.

**Corollary — the money/voice separation rule:** religious and community organizations are extraordinary legitimacy assets and terrible fiduciaries — not because they are dishonest, but because **a payment dispute involving a church or mosque is unrecoverable**. Give them enrollment endorsement, product-design consultation, grievance panels, and payout witnessing. Give them **no** premium collection, no commission, and no claims discretion.

---

## 5. Channel Archetypes: Capability Scorecard

| Channel | Effective CAC | Fiduciary trust | Index-dispute capacity | Persistency lever | Portfolio hazard |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cooperative (cash crop)** | $0.60–1.20 | High where audited | High — local knowledge | Very high (deducted at harvest settlement) | Adverse selection at coop level; concentration in one crop |
| **MNO / mobile-money agent** | $0.30–0.80 | High for *transactions*, low for *promises* | Low | Medium (auto-debit, but easy to cancel) | Mass lapse risk; MNO controls the customer |
| **MFI / SHG federation** | $0.50–1.10 | Medium-high | Medium | Very high (bundled to loan cycle) | Correlation with credit book; coercion/mis-selling risk |
| **Fintech app (standalone)** | $6–14 | Low | Very low | Low | Not viable; deprioritize |
| **Fintech app (rider on existing wallet)** | $0.40–1.00 | Inherits host | Low | Medium | Host dependency |
| **Religious / community group** | n/a | **High legitimacy, unusable as fiduciary** | **Very high** | High (social reinforcement) | Reputational contagion if implicated in a dispute |
| **Input dealer / agro-retailer** | $0.80–1.60 | Medium |
